I would love to donate one of mine, but I do not have health insurance, and while the recipients insurance might pay for my costs, many will not. The main reason I don't go through with it is the fact that if I were to donate my kidney, if somewhere down the line I needed another kidney because my single one is failing -- I'm not bumped to the top of the list for having previously donated a kidney -- which I believe should be something that is mandatory. Dialysis costs way way more than what I think the reimbursement would call for. Curious your thoughts on this.
Why do almost all countries disallow donating a kidney in exchange for money while allowing many other donations for reimbursement?

You can donate eggs, sperm, womb, blood, plasma, bone marrow, breast milk, placentas, and hair on your own volition

Most of these are a group of cells; not entire organs.

As for the womb, you only get paid if your a surrogate mother. This means that the womb stays with the donor. The only time a baby was successfully delivered after the organ was transfered from one person to another was in 2014. And I doubt in that case the donor was compensated with dollar, dollar bills y'all.

Everything in your list can be regrown or causes no effect on longevity or health, in addition to not requiring invasive surgery (although marrow donation can be quite painful from what I understand). As mentioned above, they are groups of cells, not entire organs.

That said, I believe wholeheartedly that everyone should be an organ donor. To the point where I'm not even sure it should be a choice; if your hearth could save someone and you're dead, your preferences/religion/emotional family members be damned.

There are other ethical concerns, including tie ins to human trafficking, that would arise from the ability to sell body parts. Should an 18 year old be able to sell his kidney for an X-Box?

If at any point in time kidney donation does become an option, there should be no compensation for the donor (much like blood) and the organization harvesting the kidney should provide for all of the expenses (who would then presumably be reimbursed for them by the recipient's insurance).

If you're interested in learning more, you can also draw many parallels with the problems with selling babies.

Finally, there's a VERY big precedent for not allowing donors (of anything, from blood to furniture) to contact those who receive their donations. It can cause all sorts of unwelcome behavior and situations.
